posts.title: GQA: The Memory Trick Behind Fast LLM Serving
posts.subtitle: Why Llama 3 and Mistral share key/value heads across groups of query heads instead of giving every head its own
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention shares one key/value head across a cluster of query heads instead of giving every head its own, shrinking the KV cache and speeding up serving with only a small quality cost — which is why it's the default in Llama 2/3, Mistral, and most modern open LLMs.

slides.title: One KV Cache, Shared By Many Query Heads
slides.body: Most modern open LLMs don't give every attention head its own key/value pair anymore — they share.
bullets: Used in Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral, and most modern open-weight LLMs
Sits between two older extremes: full multi-head and single shared-head attention

slides.title: The KV Cache Is What Makes Serving Expensive
slides.body: In standard multi-head attention (MHA), each of H attention heads keeps its own key (K) and value (V) vectors for every token generated so far.
bullets: KV cache size scales with number of heads × sequence length × batch size — not with model weight size
That cache, not the model weights, is often what limits how many concurrent requests a GPU can actually serve
Longer conversations and bigger batches make the problem worse, not better

slides.title: Multi-Query, Then Grouped-Query
slides.body: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) tried the extreme fix: one shared KV head for every query head — big memory savings, but a noticeable quality drop. GQA (Ainslie et al., Google, 2023) is the tunable middle ground.
bullets: Query heads are split into G groups; every head in a group shares one KV head, where 1 < G < H
Existing MHA checkpoints can be converted via 'uptraining' — mean-pooling grouped heads' K/V projections, then continuing pretraining on roughly 5% of the original compute
G is a dial: G close to H behaves like MHA, G close to 1 behaves like MQA

slides.title: Three Points on the Same Dial
bullets: H = total attention heads, G = number of shared KV groups

slides.title: Llama 2 70B's 8:1 Ratio
slides.body: Llama 2 70B uses 64 query heads but only 8 KV heads — an 8:1 grouping ratio instead of 64 separate KV heads.
bullets: KV cache memory scales with the number of KV heads, so 8 heads instead of 64 cuts that memory roughly 8x at the same sequence length and batch size
Mistral 7B pairs a similar GQA setup (32 query heads, 8 KV heads) with sliding-window attention for extra memory savings
That freed-up memory is what lets a server pack more concurrent sequences onto the same GPU

slides.title: Where the Dial Can Go Wrong
slides.body: GQA isn't a free lunch — it's a tradeoff you're choosing a point on.
bullets: Push G too low and you reprise MQA's quality loss, especially on tasks needing fine per-head specialization
The right group count is workload- and model-specific, and typically found empirically rather than by formula
Converting a pretrained MHA model to GQA needs the uptraining step — you can't just drop KV heads at inference time without retraining

slides.title: Check the Ratio, Not Just the Params
slides.body: GQA is now the default choice for serving-oriented open LLMs because it keeps most of MHA's quality at a fraction of MQA's memory footprint.
bullets: A model card's `num_key_value_heads` vs `num_attention_heads` tells you exactly where it sits on the MHA–MQA dial
Fewer KV heads means more concurrent requests per GPU, all else equal
It's an inference-serving optimization, not a training-time accuracy trick

questions.prompt: What problem does Grouped-Query Attention primarily address?
options: Slow tokenizer throughput on long documents
The KV cache's memory footprint during inference
Poor quality of training data
Limits on positional encoding range
questions.explanation: The KV cache — not the model's weights — is often the binding constraint on how many requests a GPU can serve at once. GQA shrinks it by sharing KV heads across groups of query heads.

questions.prompt: How does GQA relate to Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA)?
options: It's identical to MQA
It's a tunable middle ground — grouping query heads to share a smaller number of KV heads, between MHA's one-per-head and MQA's single shared head
It adds more KV heads than MHA uses
It removes the attention mechanism entirely
questions.explanation: GQA groups query heads into clusters that each share one KV head — a dial you can set anywhere between MHA (one KV head per query head, G=H) and MQA (a single shared KV head, G=1).

questions.prompt: In Llama 2 70B, using 8 KV heads instead of 64 does what to KV cache memory, holding sequence length and batch size fixed?
options: Increases it roughly 8x
Roughly cuts it 8x
Has no effect on memory, only on output quality
Eliminates the KV cache entirely
questions.explanation: KV cache size scales with the number of KV heads, so going from 64 separate heads to 8 shared groups cuts that memory roughly 8x, letting more sequences fit in the same GPU memory.

posts.title: Miles v0.1: Decoupling RL Rollout From Training
posts.subtitle: Why the fastest RL post-training loop is the one that never waits
posts.summary: Miles v0.1, from RadixArk (the SGLang team's spinoff, built on Tsinghua's slime), redesigns the LLM RL post-training loop so rollout generation and training run fully asynchronously instead of lockstep, reporting 3x rollout throughput, 10x faster weight sync, and 30x faster weight conversion.

slides.title: The RL Loop Has Three Stages. Most Frameworks Run Them in Lockstep.
slides.body: Generate rollouts, train on them, sync the updated weights back to the rollout engines. Miles v0.1 asks: what if none of these had to wait for the others?

slides.title: Rollout Generation Dominates Wall-Clock Time — and Idles the Trainer
slides.body: In a synchronous RL loop, the trainer GPUs sit idle while the rollout engine generates trajectories, and the rollout engines sit idle while the trainer updates weights. Since rollout generation is the slowest stage, that idle time compounds every step.
bullets: Lockstep scheduling: generate → train → sync, one stage at a time
Whichever stage is slowest sets the pace for both sets of GPUs
At frontier scale (MoE models, long trajectories), that waste is expensive hardware sitting idle

slides.title: Fully Asynchronous RL: Generate and Train Concurrently
slides.body: Miles decouples rollout (built on SGLang) from training (Megatron-LM or PyTorch FSDP), orchestrated over Ray. In async mode, rollout engines keep generating trajectories continuously; the trainer consumes whichever trajectories are finished whenever it needs its next batch.
bullets: Rollout engine: SGLang — keeps producing trajectories nonstop
Trainer: Megatron-LM or FSDP — pulls a batch whenever it's ready, no waiting
Three weight-sync transports, chosen per deployment topology (colocated vs. disaggregated GPU pools)

slides.title: The Reported Gains: 3x, 10x, 30x
slides.body: Compared to the earlier lockstep design, RadixArk reports large, stage-specific speedups — the biggest gain is in weight conversion, the mechanical step of reshaping trained weights back into a format the rollout engine can load.

slides.title: Worked Example: Training a MoE Model With GRPO
slides.body: Say you're running GRPO post-training on a large mixture-of-experts model. In the old lockstep design, the trainer finishes a step and then waits ~30-60s while weights get converted and pushed to every rollout worker before generation can resume.
bullets: Async mode: rollout workers keep generating on the previous policy version while conversion happens in the background
The trainer immediately starts consuming newly-finished trajectories for its next batch — no dead time
Miles supports GRPO, GSPO, PPO, REINFORCE++, plus SFT and on-policy distillation, on the same stack

slides.title: The Tradeoff: Staleness
slides.body: Async throughput isn't free. A rollout generated while the trainer was mid-update was sampled from a slightly older policy than the one it's eventually trained against — a staleness gap that grows if training falls behind generation.
bullets: More staleness = faster throughput but a noisier training signal
Not worth the added system complexity for small-scale, single-GPU fine-tuning jobs
Runs on NVIDIA GB300/GB200/B300/B200/H200/H100/A100 and AMD MI300X/MI325/MI350/MI355X via ROCm — but tuning the async schedule per cluster is nontrivial

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The RL post-training loop has 3 stages: rollout, train, sync weights — Miles's core idea is decoupling them instead of running them in lockstep
SGLang handles rollout, Megatron-LM/FSDP handles training, Ray orchestrates — with 3 weight-sync transports for different cluster topologies

questions.prompt: In a synchronous (lockstep) RL post-training loop, why do trainer GPUs sit idle?

They run out of memory during rollout generation
Megatron-LM requires a manual restart between steps
SGLang blocks all GPU access during inference

questions.prompt: What is the main tradeoff Miles's fully asynchronous mode introduces?

Inability to run on AMD hardware

options: Rollout throughput (3x)
Weight synchronization (10x)

Model accuracy (2x)

slides.title: Your Photo Library Just Got an Agent With Write Access

slides.title: Before: Search and Ask. Not Do.
slides.body: Photo libraries have grown into unsorted archives of tens of thousands of images. Prior AI features in Google Photos could answer a question about your library ("find photos from the beach trip") but couldn't act on the answer for you.
bullets: Finding the right photos was still manual, then curating an album was still manual
Turning a photo of an event flyer into an actual calendar entry required you to do it by hand
Sharing meant you selecting photos, creating the album, and sending it yourself

slides.title: What Changed: Spark Can Execute the Whole Workflow

bullets: One prompt can chain multiple steps: find → curate → album → share
Recurring workflows: e.g., auto-create a shared album every time you tag a new trip
Extracts text from images — a photographed flyer can become structured info

Spark plans the multi-step sequence, then asks for confirmation before the sharing step executes
Rolling out gradually: Google AI Pro/Ultra subscribers, US only, English only, 18+

slides.title: Old Assistant vs. Gemini Spark
slides.body: The jump is from a Q&A layer to an agent that plans and executes multi-step actions across the product.

posts.title: Idempotency Keys: Making Retries Safe
posts.subtitle: How to retry a network call without accidentally charging someone twice
posts.summary: An idempotency key lets a client safely retry a request that may or may not have already succeeded, by giving the server a way to recognize "this is the same operation" and return the original result instead of executing it again.

slides.title: Idempotency Keys: Making Retries Safe
slides.body: A network timeout doesn't tell you whether the server processed your request or not. Retrying blindly can be dangerous — idempotency keys make it safe.

slides.title: The Ambiguity Every Retry Faces
slides.body: You call POST /charge, the connection drops before the response arrives. Did the charge go through? You genuinely don't know — the request could have failed before reaching the server, or succeeded and only the response got lost.
bullets: Retrying is the obvious fix for transient failures — but if the original request actually succeeded, retrying re-executes it
For a payment, that means charging the customer twice
For an inventory decrement, that means double-counting a sale

slides.title: The Mechanism: A Key That Deduplicates Intent
slides.body: The client generates a unique key (typically a UUID) once per logical operation and sends it with every attempt, including retries. The server stores the key alongside the operation's result, atomically with the operation itself.
bullets: First request with a new key: server executes it, stores result keyed by that ID
Retry with the same key: server sees it's already been handled and returns the stored result — no re-execution
The key must be generated once per intent and reused across retries, never regenerated per attempt

slides.title: Worked Example: A Payment API Under Timeout
slides.body: A client calls POST /v1/charges with header Idempotency-Key: 7e9a...-4b2. The request times out client-side after 5s, but the server actually finished processing it in 6s. The client retries with the SAME key.
bullets: Server checks its idempotency table: key already exists with status=completed → returns the stored charge result immediately, doesn't charge again

Race condition: two retries arrive concurrently before the first finishes. A unique constraint on the key column plus a status=pending row (inserted before execution starts) makes the second request see a conflict and wait or return "in progress"
This pattern is exactly how Stripe's Idempotency-Key header works in production

slides.title: Naive Retry vs. Idempotency-Key Retry
slides.body: The difference shows up exactly when it matters: the request that ambiguously "maybe succeeded."

slides.title: Pitfalls to Watch For
slides.body: Idempotency keys aren't a free safety net — they need deliberate handling at the edges.
bullets: Key reused with a DIFFERENT request body: the server should reject this (or hash the body and compare) rather than silently returning a mismatched cached result
Unbounded key storage grows forever — keys need a TTL (e.g., 24h) after which they're purged and can be reused
GET requests are naturally idempotent already — idempotency keys matter for POST/PATCH/DELETE with side effects, not reads
Doesn't help across different logical operations — it only protects retries of the SAME operation, not overall business-logic consistency

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A network failure means "unknown outcome," not "failed" — safe retries need a way to detect duplicate intent
Client generates one key per logical operation; server stores key → result atomically with the side effect
Retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of re-executing — this is what makes it safe to retry payments and other side-effecting calls
Guard the edges: reject mismatched bodies on key reuse, use a unique constraint to close the concurrent-retry race, and expire keys with a TTL
This is exactly the mechanism behind Stripe's and most payment APIs' Idempotency-Key header

questions.prompt: Why is blindly retrying a failed POST /charge request risky?
options: POST requests are always rejected by servers on retry
The original request may have actually succeeded before the response was lost, so retrying could charge the customer twice
Retries always take longer than the original request
It only works over HTTP/1.1, not HTTP/2
questions.explanation: A timeout or dropped connection is ambiguous — the server may have already processed the request. Retrying without a deduplication mechanism can re-execute a side effect that already happened.

questions.prompt: How does an idempotency key prevent a duplicate charge on retry?
options: It encrypts the request body so the server can't read it twice
The server stores the key with the operation's result; a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of re-executing
It slows down the retry so the first request always finishes first
It converts the POST into a GET request
questions.explanation: The server atomically records the key alongside the executed operation's outcome. On a retry carrying the same key, it recognizes the duplicate intent and returns the cached result rather than running the operation again.

questions.prompt: What should a server do if it receives the same idempotency key with a DIFFERENT request body?
options: Execute the new body and overwrite the old cached result
Reject it (or detect the mismatch by hashing the body) instead of returning a cached result for an unrelated payload
Ignore the key entirely and always execute
Merge both request bodies into one operation
questions.explanation: Reusing a key for a different payload is a client bug or an attempted key collision — the server should reject the mismatch rather than silently returning a cached result for the wrong operation.

posts.title: Ring Attention: Near-Infinite Context Across Many GPUs
posts.subtitle: Split the sequence into blocks, rotate the key/value blocks around a ring, and hide the network transfer behind the compute.
posts.summary: Ring Attention arranges GPUs in a ring and rotates key/value blocks around it while each device keeps computing partial attention, so the maximum context length scales with the number of devices instead of any single GPU's memory. It reuses FlashAttention's blockwise, online-softmax trick and overlaps communication with compute so the ring adds little overhead when tuned correctly.

slides.title: One GPU's memory shouldn't cap how much context a model can use
slides.body: Ring Attention (Liu, Zaharia, Abbeel, UC Berkeley, 2023) arranges GPUs in a ring and rotates key/value blocks around it, so context length scales with the number of devices instead of any single device's memory.
bullets: From "Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context"
Builds on blockwise, memory-efficient attention — the same core idea behind FlashAttention
Used to train and serve models with context windows far beyond what fits on one GPU

slides.title: Self-attention's memory grows with the sequence, GPUs don't
slides.body: Every extra token in the context adds to the key/value state attention has to hold, but a GPU's HBM is fixed — so context length has always been capped by whatever fits on one device.
bullets: Standard multi-head attention needs every query to see every key/value pair in the sequence
Data or tensor parallelism doesn't fix this — each device still needs the full sequence's K/V to compute attention correctly
Naively gathering all K/V onto one device to run attention defeats the point of spreading work across GPUs

slides.title: Arrange devices in a ring, rotate the K/V blocks
slides.body: Ring Attention splits the sequence into blocks, gives each device one block's queries plus one block's keys/values, and passes K/V blocks around a ring of devices while every device keeps computing partial attention against whatever block just arrived.
bullets: Device i starts holding query block i and key/value block i
Each step, every device sends its current K/V block to the next device in the ring and receives the previous device's block
After every device has rotated through all blocks once, each query block has attended to the entire sequence

slides.title: Why the ring communication is (almost) free
slides.body: The trick is overlap: while a device waits for the next K/V block to arrive over the network, it's still finishing the attention math on the block it already has — so the transfer hides behind compute instead of stalling it.
bullets: Block size is chosen so per-block compute time is comparable to, or longer than, the ring transfer time
Blockwise, online-softmax accumulation (FlashAttention's trick) lets each device update a running result instead of needing the full row of attention scores at once
Each device only ever holds one incoming and one outgoing K/V block — memory per device stays flat no matter how long the total sequence is

slides.title: How this differs from other ways to split a long sequence

rows: A slice of every layer's weights, but still the full sequence per device
Per-device memory — sharding the model doesn't shard the sequence
Just one rotating block of the sequence's K/V at a time
Total memory across the whole ring — grows as devices are added

slides.title: A worked example: an 8-device ring on one long document
slides.body: Splitting one long context across 8 GPUs arranged in a ring.
bullets: The document's tokens are split into 8 equal blocks; device i gets query block i, plus key/value block i to start
Over 8 rotation steps, device i's query block attends to key/value blocks i, i+1, i+2, ... wrapping around, until it has seen all 8
Each device only ever stores 1/8th of the sequence's K/V at a time — that's what lets total context size scale with the ring instead of any one card's HBM

slides.title: Where Ring Attention stops paying off
bullets: Needs fast interconnects (NVLink/InfiniBand) between ring neighbors — over a slow network the transfer no longer hides behind compute and the ring stalls
Latency accumulates: a query block still has to wait its turn through the whole ring, so very large rings add tail latency even as throughput scales

It's a training/prefill-time technique for one very long sequence — it doesn't speed up token-by-token decoding, which has its own bottlenecks (that's what PagedAttention and speculative decoding target)
For sequences that already fit comfortably on one GPU, the added communication and orchestration complexity isn't worth it

slides.title: What to actually take from this
bullets: Ring Attention turns context length into a function of total devices, not any single GPU's memory, by rotating K/V blocks around a ring
It reuses FlashAttention's blockwise, online-softmax trick so no device ever needs the full attention matrix at once
The whole design hinges on overlapping network transfer with compute — block size has to be tuned so communication hides behind computation
It's a tool for extending context at training/prefill time on multi-GPU clusters, not a decoding-speed optimization

questions.prompt: At any point during Ring Attention, what does each device hold?
options: The full sequence's entire K/V cache
Just one rotating block of the sequence's K/V, plus its own fixed query block
Only the model weights, no sequence data
A compressed summary of the entire sequence
questions.explanation: Ring Attention keeps memory per device flat by only ever holding one incoming/outgoing K/V block alongside a fixed query block — this is what lets context length scale with the number of devices instead of any single GPU's memory.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the ring's network transfer stall the computation?
options: It does stall — Ring Attention is slower than single-GPU attention on every workload
Devices skip most of the attention computation to save time
Block sizes are tuned so each device's compute time overlaps with the time it takes to receive the next K/V block
It only runs on a single GPU, so there is no network transfer involved
questions.explanation: The design overlaps the K/V block transfer with attention compute on the block already in hand, hiding communication behind compute as long as block size is tuned so compute time is at least as long as transfer time.

questions.prompt: When is Ring Attention the wrong tool to reach for?
options: When training on sequences that already fit on one GPU, or when the interconnect between devices is slow
When you have exactly one GPU available and no long sequences
Whenever the model uses attention at all
Only when using Mixture-of-Experts models
questions.explanation: Ring Attention adds real communication and orchestration overhead that only pays off once the sequence doesn't fit on a single device and the ring has fast interconnects; on short sequences or slow networks it's a net loss over plain FlashAttention.

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Fixing RAG's Chunking Blind Spot
posts.subtitle: Give every chunk back the context it lost when you split the document
posts.summary: Contextual Retrieval prepends an LLM-written summary of where a chunk sits in its source document before embedding and indexing it, fixing the ambiguity that plain chunking creates. Anthropic reported it cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35% alone, 49% combined with BM25, and 67% combined with reranking, made affordable by prompt caching the source document once.

slides.title: A chunk out of context is a chunk that can't be found
slides.body: Standard RAG splits documents into chunks and embeds each one alone. That works until a chunk needs the rest of the document to mean anything.

slides.title: Chunking strips out the referent
slides.body: A 200-token chunk reads perfectly inside its source document and means almost nothing once it's isolated for embedding.
bullets: Chunk text: "The company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter." Which company? Which quarter?
The embedding model only sees that chunk — it has no way to recover the missing subject
A query for "Acme Corp Q2 2026 revenue growth" can rank this chunk low or miss it entirely
Bigger chunks reduce the problem but blow up embedding cost and dilute relevance

slides.title: Prepend context before you embed or index
slides.body: For each chunk, an LLM reads the whole source document and writes a short blurb placing that chunk in context — then the blurb is prepended to the chunk before it's embedded and indexed.
bullets: Contextual Embeddings: prepend ~50-100 tokens of chunk-specific context, then embed as usual
Contextual BM25: index that same contextualized text in a keyword/BM25 store too, not just the vector store
Example context: "This chunk is from Acme Corp's Q2 2026 10-Q, in the revenue section." + original chunk text
Retrieval still returns the original chunk to the model — the context is only there to make it findable

slides.title: Prompt caching is what makes this affordable
slides.body: Generating context for every chunk sounds like it means re-reading the whole document once per chunk — that would be brutally expensive at indexing time.
bullets: Cache the full source document once, then reuse that cached context for every chunk's context-generation call
Anthropic reported the one-time cost at roughly $1.02 per million tokens of source documents using Claude prompt caching
Without caching, the same job costs on the order of 10x more — caching is what turns this from impractical to routine
It's an indexing-time cost, not a query-time one: it happens when you build the index, not when a user asks a question

slides.title: Each layer compounds the retrieval gain
slides.body: Measured as the failure rate of the top-20 retrieved chunks on Anthropic's internal benchmark — lower is better, and the drop is cumulative.

slides.title: Worked example: a contract review assistant
slides.body: A legal team indexes 400 vendor contracts. A user asks: "What's the termination notice period in the Globex master services agreement?"
bullets: Raw chunk: "Either party may terminate this Agreement upon 60 days' written notice." — no company name, no doc title in sight
With contextual retrieval, the indexed text becomes: "From the Globex Master Services Agreement, Section 9 (Termination): Either party may terminate this Agreement upon 60 days' written notice."
Now both the embedding and the BM25 keyword match on "Globex" and "Master Services Agreement" pull this exact chunk into the top results
Without the added context, that chunk competes on identical generic termination language against dozens of other contracts and often loses

slides.title: When it's not worth it
slides.body: Contextual Retrieval adds a real indexing pipeline step — it's not free, and it's not the right fix for every RAG problem.
bullets: Small corpora (a handful of short, self-contained docs) rarely have the ambiguity problem this solves — skip it
Keep the generated context short (50-100 tokens); a long context can dilute the chunk's own embedding signal
Requires a model/provider that supports prompt caching well, or the indexing cost estimate above no longer holds
It's additive with reranking, not a replacement for it — the biggest gain (67%) comes from combining both, not either alone

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Chunking breaks the context a chunk needs to be found — Contextual Retrieval writes that context back in before indexing
It touches both the vector index (Contextual Embeddings) and the keyword index (Contextual BM25)
Prompt caching the source document is what keeps the one-time indexing cost low (~$1.02/M tokens)
Stack it with reranking for the largest measured improvement (67% fewer failed retrievals) rather than treating it as either/or

questions.prompt: What does Contextual Retrieval add to each chunk before it's embedded and indexed?
options: A random unique identifier for deduplication
A short LLM-written blurb describing where the chunk sits in its source document
A summary of the user's query
A translation of the chunk into English
questions.explanation: The technique prepends chunk-specific context (e.g. which document and section a chunk came from) generated by reading the full document, so the chunk carries enough context to be matched correctly on its own.

questions.prompt: Why does prompt caching matter for Contextual Retrieval?
options: It speeds up the user's query at runtime
It lets the model skip generating context for short chunks
It avoids re-processing the entire source document from scratch for every chunk's context-generation call, keeping indexing cost low
It replaces the need for a vector database
questions.explanation: Without caching, generating context per chunk would mean repeatedly paying to process the whole document. Caching the document once and reusing it across chunk-context calls is what makes the one-time indexing cost (roughly $1.02 per million tokens) practical.

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's reported results, what combination produced the largest drop in failed top-20 retrievals?
options: Contextual Embeddings alone (35% reduction)
Contextual BM25 alone
Contextual Embeddings + Contextual BM25 (49% reduction)
Contextual Embeddings + Contextual BM25 + reranking (67% reduction)
questions.explanation: Each layer compounds: contextual embeddings alone cut failures 35%, adding contextual BM25 reached 49%, and adding a reranking pass on top reached the reported 67% reduction — the gains are additive, not competing.

posts.title: MaxKernel: Google's Agents That Write TPU Kernels
posts.subtitle: An LLM agent loop with real compiler feedback that beats hand-tuned kernels on production workloads.
posts.summary: MaxKernel (Google, Sept 2026) is a multi-agent system that writes and optimizes TPU kernels in JAX/Pallas by looping an LLM against real compiler output and hardware profiler traces instead of generating code once and hoping. On JAXBench's 50 tasks it hits a 1.58x geometric-mean speedup, and on 8 production kernels with existing human-written baselines, its agent-tuned kernels reach 2.32x versus the reference code — edging out the 2.02x that expert engineers achieved by hand.

slides.title: The last mile of AI speed is still hand-written code
slides.body: Frameworks like JAX compile most operations well, but the highest-value kernels — the ones a model spends most of its time in — still get hand-tuned by a small number of engineers who understand the hardware.
bullets: Custom TPU kernels are written in Pallas, a low-level language exposing memory tiling and the matrix unit directly
Google's MaxKernel (arXiv:2609.04523, Sept 3 2026) points LLM agents at this bottleneck instead of at chat

slides.title: Kernel tuning is expert-scarce and slow
slides.body: Writing a fast Pallas kernel means reasoning about SRAM tile sizes, matrix-unit occupancy, and memory-vs-compute tradeoffs that don't show up until you run the thing on real silicon.
bullets: A single kernel can take a specialist days of trial-and-error profiling to tune well
Most LLM code-generation setups ask a model for one shot of code and stop — no way to react to what the compiler or profiler actually reports
That one-shot pattern is exactly what earlier work (JAXBench) showed autonomous agents struggling with on TPUs

slides.title: Three agent paradigms, one shared toolbox
slides.body: MaxKernel doesn't pick one workflow — it offers three, all built from the same pool of sub-agents.
bullets: HITL (Human-in-the-Loop): the agent proposes an optimization plan, a person approves each step — best for learning Pallas or high-stakes kernels
Auto: a fully autonomous loop runs end-to-end without a human, driven by compiler and profiler metrics
Auto-Search: spins up multiple worker agents to explore the tuning space in parallel or via beam search, then keeps the best verified-correct candidate
Shared sub-agents handle planning, implementation, self-debugging, correctness testing, and hardware profiling across all three modes

slides.title: The loop runs on real hardware, not just static analysis
slides.body: What separates this from ordinary LLM code generation is that every candidate gets compiled and executed on an actual TPU before the next revision.
bullets: Generate a candidate kernel → compile it → run it on hardware → capture the profiler trace → feed the trace back to the LLM as the next prompt
The self-debugging sub-agent handles compile errors and incorrect outputs before the profiling sub-agent even gets a turn
Because feedback is a real trace, not a guess, later revisions target the actual bottleneck (e.g. an underused matrix unit) instead of guessing

slides.title: Agent-tuned kernels vs. the human baseline
slides.body: The production-kernel comparison is the headline result: on the 8 kernels where a hand-written baseline exists, MaxKernel's agents came out ahead of the humans.

slides.title: Auto-Search exploring one stubborn kernel
slides.body: Picture a fused matmul kernel that's underusing the TPU's matrix unit.
bullets: Auto-Search launches several worker agents, each trying a different tile size and memory layout in parallel
Every candidate is compiled and profiled for real; a beam search keeps only the top performers and mutates them further
A candidate that fails correctness tests is discarded immediately, regardless of how fast its (wrong) output ran
The search converges on a kernel a human might reach only after days of manual profiling sessions

slides.title: Where this approach costs you
slides.body: Running an agent loop against real hardware is not free, and the result is not a drop-in replacement for every situation.
bullets: Each iteration needs a real TPU compile-and-run cycle — this is expensive and slow compared to a single LLM code-gen call
Auto-Search's parallel exploration multiplies that hardware cost by however many workers you run
Correctness testing is load-bearing: without a solid test harness, a fast-but-wrong kernel could pass unnoticed
Not worth it for a kernel you'll run once or for teams without spare TPU capacity to burn on search

slides.title: What to remember about MaxKernel
bullets: The trick isn't a smarter prompt — it's closing the loop with a real compiler and profiler on real hardware
Three modes (HITL, Auto, Auto-Search) trade human oversight for autonomy and search breadth
On production kernels with human baselines, agent-tuned code beat the humans: 2.32x vs. 2.02x
The cost is hardware time and a trustworthy correctness harness — this is an infrastructure investment, not a free lunch

questions.prompt: What makes MaxKernel's approach different from a typical 'ask an LLM to write a kernel' setup?
options: It only works with Python instead of Pallas
It closes the loop with real compiler output and hardware profiler traces across multiple iterations
It avoids testing kernels for correctness to save time
It replaces the TPU's matrix unit with a software emulator
questions.explanation: MaxKernel's core idea is iterative: generate, compile, run on real hardware, profile, and feed that trace back into the next LLM revision — not a single one-shot generation.

questions.prompt: On the 8 production kernels with existing human-written baselines, how did MaxKernel's agents compare?
options: They matched human performance exactly
They underperformed humans by roughly 15%
They outperformed the human baseline: 2.32x vs. 2.02x geomean speedup
They could not produce correct kernels for any of the 8 tasks
questions.explanation: This is the paper's headline number: on production kernels where expert engineers had already hand-tuned a baseline, MaxKernel's agent-generated kernels reached a higher geometric-mean speedup than the human-written versions.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical cost of MaxKernel's Auto-Search mode?
options: It requires no hardware at all, running purely in simulation
It multiplies real TPU compile-and-run cycles across many parallel workers, which is expensive
It cannot handle kernels larger than a few lines of code
It only works on GPUs, not TPUs
questions.explanation: Because every candidate must actually compile and run on hardware to get a real profiler trace, running many workers in parallel (as Auto-Search does) multiplies that hardware cost — the tradeoff for a broader, faster search.

posts.title: Mistral Agentic Search: Retrieval That Checks Its Own Work
posts.subtitle: Five operations replace a single embedding lookup — and correctness on dense docs triples.
posts.summary: Mistral's Agentic Search (2026) replaces classic one-shot embed-and-retrieve RAG with a multi-step loop where the model can search, open, navigate, read, and grep through documents until it has real evidence — closer to an analyst using find-in-page than a search engine. On FinanceBench it lifts correctness from 26.7% to 86%, and on the table-heavy OfficeQA Pro benchmark it gains 45.6 points (6.3% to 51.9%), at the cost of more tool calls and latency per query.

slides.title: RAG never gets to double-check itself
slides.body: Standard retrieval-augmented generation embeds a query, pulls the top-k chunks once, and hands them to the model — there's no step where the model can say 'that number looks off, let me look again.'
bullets: Mistral shipped Agentic Search into its Search Toolkit, Libraries, Studio, and Vibe products in 2026
It's built for the documents one-shot RAG handles worst: dense filings, tables split across pages, multi-hop references

slides.title: Chunking breaks the documents that matter most
slides.body: Fixed-size chunking is a reasonable approximation for prose, but it mangles structure that spans page boundaries.
bullets: A table split mid-row across two chunks loses the row's meaning to both halves
A footnote defining a term used three pages earlier lands in a chunk nowhere near where it's needed
On FinanceBench, traditional single-shot RAG scored only 26.7% correctness — dense financial filings are exactly this kind of document
Once the wrong chunk is retrieved, the model has no mechanism to go back and check

slides.title: Five operations instead of one lookup
slides.body: Agentic Search gives the model a small toolkit and lets it keep working until it has enough evidence to answer.
bullets: search — find candidate documents or sections across the corpus
open — load a specific document
navigate — move to a particular page or section within it
read — pull the exact content at that location
grep — search for a pattern inside the document, like confirming a figure doesn't appear elsewhere with a different value

slides.title: An orchestration layer, not a new retriever
slides.body: Agentic Search sits on top of existing retrieval primitives rather than replacing them.
bullets: It adds navigation and iteration on top of standard search/embeddings, continuing the loop until the model judges it has enough evidence
Ships inside the Mistral Search Toolkit and is built into the Libraries feature, plus Studio and Vibe
Supports both cloud and on-premises deployment

slides.title: Correctness gains on structure-heavy benchmarks
slides.body: Both benchmarks stress exactly the failure mode one-shot RAG has: dense tables and multi-document, multi-hop questions.

slides.title: Finding one footnote in a 200-page filing
slides.body: Task: locate the exact gross-margin footnote in a long 10-K where the relevant table spans a page break.
bullets: search surfaces the filing as a likely candidate among the corpus
open loads the full document instead of a pre-cut chunk
navigate jumps to the financial-statements section rather than scanning linearly
read pulls the precise footnote text once located
grep checks the same figure doesn't appear elsewhere with a conflicting value before the model commits to an answer

slides.title: The loop isn't free
slides.body: Multiple tool calls per query is the price of the accuracy gain, and it isn't always worth paying.
bullets: Every search/open/navigate/read/grep step is a round trip — latency and cost scale with how many steps a question needs
Simple lookups (a short FAQ, a single well-chunked paragraph) gain little and pay the overhead anyway
Still depends on a working index and navigable document structure underneath — it orchestrates retrieval, it doesn't replace the need for one
Not a fit for latency-critical paths where a single fast embedding lookup is good enough

slides.title: What to remember about Agentic Search
bullets: It reframes retrieval as a loop the model drives, not a single embedding lookup
Five operations (search, open, navigate, read, grep) let it verify before answering, not just retrieve and hope
Biggest wins are on dense, structured, multi-hop documents — FinanceBench correctness roughly tripled
Reach for it when documents are messy and being wrong is costly; skip it for simple, latency-sensitive lookups

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between Agentic Search and traditional single-shot RAG?
options: Agentic Search uses a bigger embedding model
Agentic Search lets the model iterate — searching, navigating, and verifying — instead of retrieving once and stopping
Agentic Search removes the need for any document index
Agentic Search only works on plain text, never tables
questions.explanation: Traditional RAG embeds a query and pulls top-k chunks once. Agentic Search gives the model five operations (search, open, navigate, read, grep) and lets it keep working until it has enough evidence — closer to an analyst than a one-shot lookup.

questions.prompt: On the FinanceBench benchmark, what correctness jump did Agentic Search show over traditional RAG?
options: No meaningful change
From 26.7% to 86%
From 86% to 99%
From 50% to 60%
questions.explanation: Traditional single-shot RAG scored 26.7% correctness on FinanceBench's dense financial filings; Agentic Search reached 86% by letting the model navigate and verify instead of trusting the first retrieved chunk.

questions.prompt: When is Agentic Search's multi-step loop NOT worth using?
options: When documents are large, dense filings with tables spanning pages
For a simple, well-chunked FAQ lookup where latency matters and one retrieval already suffices
When multi-hop reasoning across several documents is required
When the answer must be verified against conflicting figures in the same corpus
questions.explanation: Every step in the loop is a round trip that adds latency and cost. For simple lookups where a single embedding retrieval already gets the right chunk, the extra steps add overhead without a meaningful accuracy gain.

posts.title: FlashAttention: Fast, Exact Attention on GPUs
posts.subtitle: Same math as standard attention, 2-4x faster, by never writing the full score matrix to slow memory.
posts.summary: FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) speeds up transformer attention not by approximating it but by rethinking which memory it touches: it tiles the computation so the full N x N attention matrix never has to leave a GPU's fast on-chip SRAM. That IO-awareness delivers 2-4x speedups and linear instead of quadratic memory, with no change to the output. FlashAttention-2 pushed further, reaching up to 230 TFLOPs/s on an A100 (73% of peak) and a 1.3x end-to-end GPT-2 training speedup over the original.

slides.title: The matrix nobody should have to build
slides.body: Standard attention computes QK^T, applies softmax, then multiplies by V — and in the middle, it materializes a full N x N matrix of attention scores.
bullets: For a sequence of 8,000 tokens, that's a 8,000 x 8,000 matrix per attention head, per batch item
FlashAttention (Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra, Ré — arXiv:2205.14135) asks: what if that matrix never has to exist in slow memory at all?

slides.title: The bottleneck is memory movement, not math
slides.body: GPUs have two very different kinds of memory, and attention's naive implementation abuses the slow one.
bullets: On-chip SRAM: extremely fast (~19 TB/s) but tiny — tens of megabytes
Off-chip HBM: large (tens of gigabytes) but far slower (~1.5-2 TB/s) to move data through
Standard attention writes the full N x N score matrix to HBM after QK^T, reads it back for softmax, then reads it again for the final multiply by V
Attention looks compute-heavy but is actually memory-bound: the GPU spends more time waiting on data movement than doing arithmetic

slides.title: Tile the computation, keep it all in SRAM
slides.body: FlashAttention splits Q, K, and V into small blocks that fit inside SRAM, and fuses the whole QK^T → softmax → weighted-sum pipeline into a single GPU kernel.
bullets: Each block of Q is compared against blocks of K and V one at a time, entirely inside fast on-chip memory
An 'online softmax' trick keeps a running max and running sum so partial results can be combined correctly without ever seeing the full row at once
The full N x N matrix is never written to HBM — only the final output and a small per-row statistic are

slides.title: The backward pass recomputes instead of storing
slides.body: Training needs the attention matrix again during backpropagation — FlashAttention doesn't store it, it recomputes it on the fly.
bullets: Only a small logsumexp statistic per row is kept from the forward pass, not the full matrix
During the backward pass, blocks of the attention matrix are recomputed from that statistic as needed — trading a bit of extra compute for a large memory saving
This 'recompute over store' choice is why the method is called IO-aware rather than an approximation — the output is mathematically identical to standard attention

slides.title: The numbers, v1 to v2
slides.body: FlashAttention-2 (2023) improved parallelism and work partitioning on top of the same core idea.

slides.title: Why this is what let context windows grow
slides.body: Training at an 8k context with standard attention means repeatedly moving a ~256MB (per head, fp32) score matrix through HBM — brutal on bandwidth, and often just not fitting in memory at all.
bullets: FlashAttention instead processes, say, 128-row/128-column tiles that comfortably fit in a GPU SM's SRAM
Each tile does a small, fast matmul entirely on-chip before moving to the next one
This is a direct reason models could jump from low-thousands of tokens of context to tens of thousands without a proportional memory blowup

slides.title: Where it doesn't help, or needs redoing
slides.body: FlashAttention is not a universal free lunch.
bullets: It reduces memory traffic, not the underlying O(N²) FLOP count — it doesn't fix attention's asymptotic scaling the way sub-quadratic methods (linear attention, Mamba) aim to
On short sequences (roughly under 512 tokens), tiling overhead eats into the gains — the wins compound with sequence length
It's tied to specific GPU architectures — Hopper's async instructions and FP8 support needed a dedicated FlashAttention-3 to exploit
It's exact, which is the point — don't reach for it expecting the further speedups that come from approximate/sparse attention variants

slides.title: What to remember about FlashAttention
bullets: The bottleneck it solves is memory bandwidth (SRAM vs. HBM traffic), not raw compute
Tiling plus online softmax means the full N x N score matrix never touches slow memory
It's mathematically exact — zero accuracy tradeoff, unlike sparse or linear attention approximations
FlashAttention-2 reached up to 230 TFLOPs/s on A100 (73% of peak) and a 1.3x end-to-end training speedup over v1
Gains grow with sequence length and are architecture-specific — newer GPUs need their own kernel version

questions.prompt: What is the actual bottleneck FlashAttention targets in standard attention?
options: The number of floating-point operations (FLOPs) required
Memory bandwidth — repeatedly moving the full attention matrix between slow HBM and fast SRAM
The number of attention heads in the model
The precision of the softmax function
questions.explanation: Standard attention looks compute-heavy but is memory-bound: it writes and reads the full N x N score matrix to slow HBM multiple times. FlashAttention's tiling keeps that traffic inside fast on-chip SRAM instead.

questions.prompt: Is FlashAttention an approximation of standard attention?
options: Yes, it drops small attention weights to save time
Yes, it uses a sparse pattern that skips some tokens
No — it produces mathematically identical output; only the memory access pattern changes
No, but it changes the softmax formula to a faster approximation
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is IO-aware, not approximate. Tiling plus the online softmax trick and recomputation in the backward pass produce exactly the same result as standard attention — the speedup comes purely from avoiding unnecessary memory movement.

questions.prompt: According to the FlashAttention-2 paper, roughly what throughput did it reach on an A100 GPU, and what was the end-to-end GPT-2 training speedup over the original FlashAttention?
options: 10 TFLOPs/s, and a 10x training speedup
Up to 230 TFLOPs/s (73% of peak), and a 1.3x end-to-end training speedup
500 TFLOPs/s, and no measurable training speedup
230 TFLOPs/s, but training became slower due to overhead
questions.explanation: FlashAttention-2 reached up to 230 TFLOPs/s on A100 (about 73% of the theoretical peak) and delivered a 1.3x end-to-end speedup training GPT-style models compared to the original FlashAttention, and 2.8x versus a baseline without it.

posts.title: HNSW: Fast Approximate Search Over Millions of Vectors
posts.subtitle: A layered graph inspired by skip lists turns nearest-neighbor search from a linear scan into a handful of hops.
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based algorithm behind most production vector search — Faiss, hnswlib, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant, and pgvector all build on it. It arranges vectors into a multi-layer graph where sparse upper layers let a query take long jumps and the dense bottom layer refines the answer, turning search into roughly log(N) hops instead of a full scan. It trades a small, tunable amount of recall for that speed, and pays for it in RAM and slow deletes.

slides.title: A skip list, but for nearest neighbors
slides.body: HNSW (Malkov & Yashunin, 2016) is the graph structure most vector databases build under the hood — Faiss, hnswlib, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant, and pgvector's `hnsw` index all use it.
bullets: Turns 'find the closest vector to this one' from a full scan into a handful of graph hops
No training step required — unlike clustering-based indexes, you just insert vectors one at a time
The default choice when you need high recall at low latency and can afford the RAM

slides.title: Comparing a query to every vector doesn't scale
slides.body: Brute-force nearest-neighbor search is exact but linear — every added vector adds a fixed amount of work to every future query.
bullets: A brute-force scan over 10 million 768-dim embeddings means 10 million distance computations per query
Even at roughly a microsecond per comparison, that's already single-digit milliseconds of pure compute per query, before reranking or generation even starts
High-dimensional distance doesn't compress with simple tricks like sorting or hashing — you need structure, not a shortcut

slides.title: Layers get sparser as you go up, like a skip list
slides.body: HNSW builds a graph where every vector lives on layer 0, but only a shrinking fraction also exists on higher layers.
bullets: Each inserted point is randomly assigned a top layer, with the probability of reaching the next layer up decaying exponentially — layer 0 might hold 10M points while layer 4 holds a few hundred
On every layer, a node connects to roughly M of its nearest already-inserted neighbors (a common default is M=16)
Higher layers act like highways for long jumps across the vector space; layer 0 is the dense, fine-grained local map

slides.title: Search greedily descends, then runs a local beam search
slides.body: A query starts at a fixed entry point on the top layer and works its way down.
bullets: At each layer, greedily hop to whichever neighbor is closest to the query until no neighbor is closer — that local minimum becomes the entry point for the layer below

At layer 0, instead of stopping at one point, HNSW keeps a candidate list of size ef (efSearch) and keeps expanding the best unexplored candidates — this beam search is what makes results approximate rather than purely greedy
Total hops scale roughly with log(N): doubling the dataset adds about one more layer to cross, not double the work

slides.title: HNSW vs. brute-force vs. IVF
slides.body: IVF (Inverted File Index) clusters vectors with k-means and only searches the nprobe closest clusters; HNSW skips training entirely but pays for it in RAM.

slides.title: A RAG retriever answering under 20ms
slides.body: Concrete setup: 5 million document chunks embedded at 1536 dimensions, stored in an HNSW index with M=16, efConstruction=200.
bullets: Brute-force: ~5M distance computations per query — tens of milliseconds of pure math before reranking even starts
HNSW with efSearch=50: a few hundred distance computations spread across roughly 4-5 layers — typically single-digit milliseconds
Raise efSearch to 200 for a hard query that needs higher recall — it's a per-query knob you tune live, not something that requires rebuilding the index

slides.title: The RAM bill and the missing delete button
slides.body: HNSW's speed comes from a graph that has to live in memory, and that graph doesn't like being edited.
bullets: Index size typically runs 1.5-2x the raw vector data, since every node stores M+ neighbor pointers per layer on top of the vector itself
Deleting a vector doesn't remove it from other nodes' neighbor lists — implementations usually tombstone it and filter at query time, or require a periodic rebuild
Recall is probabilistic, not guaranteed: a query can genuinely miss the true nearest neighbor, so HNSW is the wrong tool when you need exact results (e.g. deduplication) instead of 'close enough'
When data won't fit in RAM, a disk-oriented index like DiskANN trades some latency for handling billions of vectors off SSD

slides.title: What to remember about HNSW
bullets: It's a layered graph — sparse on top for long jumps, dense at the bottom for fine-grained search, like a skip list for vectors
Three knobs matter: M (graph density/memory), efConstruction (build-time quality), efSearch (query-time recall vs. speed)
It trades a small, tunable amount of recall for roughly logarithmic query time and zero training step
Watch the RAM budget, and avoid it when you need exact results or a workload with heavy deletes/updates

questions.prompt: What does the parameter efSearch control in HNSW?
options: The number of layers in the graph
The size of the candidate list explored at query time, trading speed for recall
The dimensionality of the stored vectors
The number of vectors removed per rebuild
questions.explanation: efSearch sets how many candidates HNSW keeps open while searching layer 0. A larger efSearch explores more of the graph, raising recall at the cost of more distance computations per query — and it's tunable per query, with no rebuild needed.

questions.prompt: Why does HNSW use a hierarchy of layers instead of one flat graph?
options: To store redundant copies of each vector for fault tolerance
To let long-distance jumps happen on sparse upper layers before fine-grained search on the dense bottom layer
To support multiple distance metrics at once
To reduce the dimensionality of vectors before comparison
questions.explanation: The layered structure mirrors a skip list: sparse upper layers let a search cross the vector space in a few big hops, then progressively denser layers refine the answer — that's what keeps search close to logarithmic instead of linear in the number of vectors.

questions.prompt: Which workload is HNSW a poor fit for?
options: Powering a RAG retriever over a mostly-static document set
Semantic search over a few million product descriptions
A dataset with heavy continuous deletes and updates
A recommendation system doing lookups on stable embeddings
questions.explanation: HNSW graphs don't support cheap deletes — removing a node still leaves dangling references in its neighbors' edge lists, so implementations typically tombstone entries and periodically rebuild. Workloads with constant churn pay for that maintenance repeatedly.

posts.title: Mamba: Ditching Attention for a Constant-Size State
posts.subtitle: Selective state space models process sequences in linear time with a fixed-size memory — no KV cache required.
posts.summary: Mamba replaces self-attention with a selective state space model: a recurrence whose update rule depends on the current token, computed via a hardware-aware parallel scan. It runs in linear time with a constant-size hidden state instead of a growing KV cache, trading some precise long-range recall for far cheaper long-sequence inference.

slides.title: Attention scales quadratically. Mamba doesn't.
slides.body: Mamba (Albert Gu and Tri Dao, December 2023) replaces self-attention with a selective state space model — a recurrence that updates a fixed-size hidden state instead of attending over every past token.
bullets: No attention, no KV cache — just a hidden state that updates one token at a time
Runs in linear time and constant memory per generated token
Now the backbone (often mixed with attention) of long-context and on-device models

slides.title: Every generated token costs more than the last one did
slides.body: Self-attention's cost and memory both grow with how much context the model has already seen.
bullets: Self-attention compares every token to every other token: O(n^2) compute over a sequence of length n
Autoregressive decoding keeps a KV cache — one key and value vector per past token — that grows linearly with the conversation
Past a few hundred thousand tokens, that KV cache can occupy more GPU memory than the model's own weights

slides.title: A state space model keeps a summary, not a list
slides.body: The idea predates deep learning: control theory describes a system by a hidden state that evolves over time.
bullets: A continuous-time SSM updates a hidden state h via matrices A, B, C, then reads it out through C — discretized into a step-by-step recurrence for use on sequences

Earlier structured SSMs (S4, 2021) kept A, B, C fixed for the entire sequence, which let the recurrence be rewritten as one big convolution — fast, but the same fixed matrices had to work for every input
That fixed-parameter constraint made S4 efficient but weak at content-based behavior like 'copy this token' or 'ignore that one'

slides.title: Mamba makes the update depend on the input
slides.body: Mamba's fix: let the SSM's parameters change based on what token it's currently looking at.
bullets: B, C, and the timestep Delta become functions of the current token, so the model can choose what to remember or forget based on content — this is the 'selective' in selective SSM
That breaks the fixed-kernel convolution trick S4 relied on, so Mamba instead computes the recurrence with a hardware-aware parallel scan
The scan keeps the large intermediate state in fast GPU SRAM instead of spilling it to slower HBM — the same IO-awareness idea behind FlashAttention
Net effect: a genuinely input-dependent recurrent model that still trains at near-Transformer speed on GPUs

slides.title: Where each architecture wins on paper

rows: KV cache grows linearly with tokens seen
Fixed-size hidden state that never grows
Strong — any past token stays directly addressable
Weaker — history is compressed into the fixed state

slides.title: Reading a 400,000-token document on one GPU
slides.body: The constant-memory property is easiest to see with a concrete scale.
bullets: A Transformer reading that document keeps a growing KV cache entry for every one of those 400,000 tokens
A Mamba-based model updates the same fixed-size hidden state the whole way through — memory use at token 400,000 looks identical to memory use at token 400
This is why SSM and hybrid layers show up specifically in models built for very long context or on-device deployment, where KV-cache memory — not raw FLOPs — is the actual limit

slides.title: Compression has a cost: exact recall gets harder
slides.body: Squeezing the whole history into one fixed-size state is not free.
bullets: Retrieving one exact fact from far back ('needle in a haystack') is harder for a compressed state than for attention, which can look at any individual past token directly
Follow-up work on in-context recall benchmarks shows pure SSMs specifically lag attention on tasks needing exact copying or lookup, even when they match it on general language modeling loss
The practical fix is hybrid architectures: interleave a handful of attention layers among mostly-SSM layers — Mistral's Codestral Mamba and AI21's Jamba both ship this way

Don't reach for a pure SSM when the task is dominated by precise long-document retrieval — that's still attention's or RAG's strength. Reach for it when raw sequence length and serving memory are the bottleneck

slides.title: What to actually take from this
bullets: Mamba swaps attention for a selective state space model: a recurrence whose update matrices depend on the current input
The payoff is O(n) compute and a constant-size state, instead of O(n^2) attention and an ever-growing KV cache
The cost is weaker exact long-range recall, which is why hybrid attention+SSM architectures exist
It matters most for very long sequences or memory-constrained serving — not as a universal attention replacement

questions.prompt: What is the core architectural change Mamba makes compared to earlier structured state space models like S4?
options: It removes the hidden state entirely
It makes the SSM's B, C, and timestep parameters depend on the current input (selective) instead of holding them fixed
It replaces the state space model with an LSTM
It adds more attention heads to the model
questions.explanation: S4 held its A, B, C matrices fixed across the whole sequence, which enabled a fast convolution but limited it to input-independent behavior. Mamba makes B, C, and the timestep depend on the current token, letting it selectively remember or forget content — at the cost of that convolution shortcut, which is why it needs a hardware-aware parallel scan instead.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't Mamba's memory usage grow as it generates more tokens, unlike a Transformer's KV cache?
options: It only keeps the last 10 tokens in memory
It stores every past token's key and value vectors, just compressed
It updates a single fixed-size hidden state at each step instead of appending to a growing cache
It offloads memory to disk automatically
questions.explanation: Mamba's recurrence updates one fixed-size hidden state per step. That state's size doesn't depend on how many tokens came before it, unlike a Transformer's KV cache, which stores a vector per past token and keeps growing.

questions.prompt: What is the main tradeoff of Mamba's fixed-size state compared to attention?
options: It cannot be trained on GPUs
It requires far more parameters than a Transformer of similar quality
Precise recall of one exact fact from far back in the sequence is harder, since history gets compressed rather than kept token-by-token
It cannot process sequences longer than 4,096 tokens
questions.explanation: Because the entire history is compressed into one fixed-size state, exact lookup of a specific past detail is harder than for attention, which can address any individual past token directly. This is why hybrid architectures mix in a few attention layers to patch the recall gap.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guess Ahead, Verify in Parallel
posts.subtitle: A cheap draft model proposes tokens; the big model checks them all in one pass.
posts.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM generation by having a small draft model propose several tokens ahead, then verifying them all in one parallel pass through the target model — with a rejection-sampling scheme that guarantees the output distribution never changes.

slides.title: Speculative Decoding: Guess Ahead, Verify in Parallel
slides.body: Autoregressive LLMs generate one token per forward pass. Speculative decoding lets a small draft model propose several tokens at once, then the big model checks them all in a single pass — same output distribution, fewer expensive passes.

slides.title: Decoding Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
bullets: Generating each token requires a full forward pass through every layer of the target model — for a 70B model that means tens of GB of weights streamed from HBM per single token.
At small batch sizes the GPU spends most of that pass waiting on memory bandwidth, not doing math — its arithmetic units sit mostly idle.
The sequential dependency between tokens means you can't start token N+1 until token N is sampled, so passes can't just be pipelined away.

slides.title: A Cheap Draft Model Proposes, the Big Model Verifies
slides.body: Run a small, fast 'draft' model autoregressively for k steps to propose k candidate tokens. Then run the large 'target' model ONCE on all k+1 positions in parallel — one memory-bound pass instead of k.
bullets: Draft model: a much smaller model from the same family (e.g., a ~1B model drafting for a 70B target), or the target itself with an early exit.
The target checks every draft token's probability under its own distribution in a single batched forward pass covering all k positions.
Accepted tokens are free wins; the first rejected token is resampled from a corrected distribution — never accepted from something the target disagrees with.

slides.title: Rejection Sampling Keeps the Output Provably Identical
slides.body: The math guarantees the sampled sequence has exactly the same distribution as sampling from the target model alone — this is a lossless speedup, not an approximation.
bullets: For each draft token, accept it with probability min(1, p_target(token) / p_draft(token)).
If rejected, resample from the residual distribution max(0, p_target − p_draft), renormalized — this exactly cancels the draft model's bias.
If all k draft tokens are accepted, sample one bonus token for free from the target's distribution at position k+1.

slides.title: Walking Through One Verification Step
slides.body: Suppose k=4 and a draft model is completing 'The capital of France is ___'. The target model checks all draft positions in one pass.
bullets: Draft proposes: 'The', 'capital', 'of', 'Spain' — the target agrees on the first three but assigns near-zero probability to 'Spain' given the earlier context.
The first 3 tokens are accepted for the cost of ONE target forward pass; the 4th is rejected and correctly resampled as 'France'.
Net result: 4 tokens advance (3 accepted + 1 resampled) using 1 expensive target pass plus 4 cheap draft passes, instead of 4 expensive target passes.

slides.title: Acceptance Rate Decides the Real-World Speedup
bullets: Speedup scales with acceptance rate — predictable text like code or boilerplate accepts far more draft tokens than creative or highly technical writing.
Real gains also depend on how much cheaper the draft pass is relative to the target pass, and how large k is set.

rows: Separate small LM drafting for a larger target
Small separate LM (e.g., 70M) drafting for a much larger target
Extra prediction heads bolted onto the target model itself
Drafts in the target's feature space one layer up, not raw tokens
Higher acceptance rate than vanilla drafting

slides.title: When It Doesn't Pay Off
bullets: Low-acceptance domains (highly creative or out-of-distribution text) mean most draft tokens get rejected — you pay for the draft passes without saving target passes.
It needs a second model resident in memory (or extra heads/layers) — added VRAM and engineering complexity, and the draft model must stay well-aligned as the target is updated.
Large-batch serving dilutes the win: the technique helps most at low batch sizes where the target pass is memory-bound and underutilized; at high batch sizes the pass is already compute-bound.
Setting k too high wastes draft compute on tokens that get rejected anyway; too low caps the ceiling on speedup — it needs tuning per workload.

slides.title: Same Output, Fewer Expensive Passes
bullets: Speculative decoding is lossless: it changes wall-clock time, not what the model would have said.
The core trick is trading many cheap draft passes for fewer expensive target passes, exploiting idle GPU capacity during memory-bound decoding.
Acceptance rate is the number that matters most — it's set by how well the draft model's distribution matches the target's on your actual traffic.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't speculative decoding change the model's output distribution?
options: It always accepts the draft model's guess
Rejected tokens are corrected with a residual resampling step that exactly cancels the draft model's bias
It only works with deterministic (greedy) decoding
The target model is skipped entirely
questions.explanation: The accept/reject rule (min(1, p_target/p_draft)) plus resampling from the residual distribution on rejection is mathematically equivalent to sampling straight from the target model — that equivalence is what makes the speedup lossless.

questions.prompt: What actually makes standard autoregressive decoding slow on a GPU?
options: The GPU runs out of arithmetic throughput
Each token requires a full memory-bound pass through the model's weights, and tokens must be generated sequentially
Tokenization is CPU-bound and dominates latency
Attention cost grows so fast it dominates every step
questions.explanation: At small batch sizes, decoding is bottlenecked on streaming weights from memory rather than on compute, and the sequential dependency between tokens prevents batching multiple steps together — exactly the idle capacity speculative decoding exploits.

questions.prompt: When does speculative decoding help the LEAST?
options: Low batch size, predictable text like code
High batch size serving, where the target's pass is already compute-bound
Long documents with repetitive structure
When the draft model closely matches the target's style
questions.explanation: At high batch sizes the target model's forward pass is already compute-bound rather than memory-bound, so there's little idle GPU capacity left for speculative decoding to soak up — the technique shines most at low batch sizes.

posts.title: Orchard: An Open Framework for Scaling Agentic AI
posts.subtitle: Microsoft's open-source stack trains agents inside the same Kubernetes sandboxes they later deploy in.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research open-sourced Orchard, a Kubernetes-native framework that trains agents inside the exact harnesses they deploy in. Its three recipes (SWE, GUI, Claw) hit strong benchmark scores with small models by closing the train-deploy gap other frameworks leave open.

slides.title: One Framework, Three Layers, Zero Train-Deploy Mismatch
bullets: Open-sourced by Microsoft Research, August 3, 2026
Kubernetes-native sandboxes for training AND deployment
Ships three ready-made agent recipes: SWE, GUI, Claw

slides.title: Agent Training Infrastructure Is a Private Luxury
slides.body: Frontier labs train agents against proprietary sandboxes, closed pipelines, and datasets nobody else can see — so most researchers can't reproduce agent RL results at all.
bullets: Custom sandboxes and closed training pipelines are the norm at big labs
A trained agent is often evaluated in a different harness than it trained in — a 'train-deploy mismatch' that quietly costs performance
Reproducible agent research needs open, reusable infrastructure, not another one-off eval script

slides.title: Orchard Env: A Kubernetes Layer Under Every Agent
slides.body: The core of Orchard is Orchard Env — a lightweight Kubernetes-native service that manages isolated sandboxes, file I/O, networking, and APIs for agents, whether they're training or running in production.
bullets: Layer 1 — Orchard Env: isolated, reusable sandboxes on Kubernetes
Layer 2 — Domain recipes: Orchard-SWE (coding), Orchard-GUI (web navigation), Orchard-Claw (personal-assistant tasks)
Layer 3 — Training pipeline: data curation, curriculum design, SFT, RL, evaluation
Agents train directly inside real deployment harnesses (Codex, OpenClaw, ZeroClaw) instead of a synthetic training-only sandbox

slides.title: Small Models, Benchmark Scores That Punch Above Their Size
bullets: Orchard-SWE approaches systems reported to be roughly 10x larger
Orchard-Claw reaches its score after training on just 200 synthetic tasks

slides.title: Training Orchard-GUI to Not Get Lost in a Website
slides.body: A concrete run: Orchard-GUI, a 4-billion-parameter vision-language model, is dropped into recipe environments and has to complete multi-step web tasks — find a product, fill a form, complete checkout — while the sandbox scores task completion automatically.
bullets: The same recipe is reused across WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and DeepShop without rebuilding infrastructure
Because training happens inside the deployment harness, the policy that ships is the exact policy that was scored
The 68.4% average is a mean across all three benchmarks — no single benchmark is cherry-picked

slides.title: The Training Loop Underneath Every Recipe
slides.body: Every Orchard recipe runs the same five-stage pipeline: curate data, design a curriculum of increasing task difficulty, supervised fine-tune on demonstrations, reinforcement-learn against the sandbox's own reward signal, then evaluate — all before the agent ever leaves Orchard Env.
bullets: Curriculum design matters as much as the RL algorithm — ramping difficulty keeps the agent from collapsing on hard tasks early
Reward comes from the sandbox itself (task completion, test pass/fail) rather than a separate learned reward model

slides.title: Where Orchard Fits — and Where It Doesn't
slides.body: Orchard is infrastructure, not a finished product: you still need to build or adapt a recipe for your domain, and its benchmark numbers come from Microsoft's own recipes, not a guarantee for arbitrary tasks.
bullets: Best fit: teams that want to train task-specific agents and need training/deployment parity
Not a fit: teams that just want to call an existing hosted agent API with no training loop of their own
Open code and datasets make it auditable, but you still own the ops burden of running Kubernetes sandboxes

slides.title: Three Things Worth Remembering
bullets: Orchard closes the train-deploy gap by training agents inside the same harness (Codex, OpenClaw, ZeroClaw) they'll run in
Small, task-specific models (3-4B active params) can approach much larger systems when the training loop matches the deployment loop
It's open infrastructure, not a hosted product — you still build the recipe and run the cluster

questions.prompt: What problem does Orchard Env solve directly?
options: It provides isolated, reusable Kubernetes sandboxes agents can train AND deploy in
It replaces the need for reinforcement learning entirely
It hosts a proprietary agent API
It only works with one specific model family
questions.explanation: Orchard Env is the Kubernetes-native layer that removes the mismatch between where an agent trains and where it deploys.

questions.prompt: How does Orchard-SWE's active parameter count compare to systems it approaches in performance?
options: About the same size
Roughly 10x smaller
100x smaller
It's actually larger
questions.explanation: Orchard-SWE uses about 3B active parameters yet approaches systems reported to be roughly 10x larger on SWE-bench Verified.

questions.prompt: Why does training inside the real deployment harness (Codex, OpenClaw, ZeroClaw) matter?
options: It makes training faster on any hardware
It avoids the need for a curriculum
It ensures the exact policy trained is the one that ships, avoiding train-deploy mismatch
It removes the need for benchmarks
questions.explanation: Training inside the same harness used at deployment means there's no gap between the environment an agent learned in and the one it operates in.
